person.name: Zaha_Hadid
person.summary: Zaha Hadid was an Iraqi British architect whose paintings, drawings, and buildings used fractured planes, flowing lines, and dramatic spatial sequences. After years of influential unbuilt projects, she led Zaha Hadid Architects to major cultural, civic, and sporting commissions around the world.

conclusion: Hadid left a body of public buildings that carries the spatial ideas first developed in her paintings and drawings. Her work includes cultural institutions, an Olympic venue, and the Vitra Fire Station, where her first built project remains an exhibition space.

events.title: Birth in Baghdad
events.description: Her father, Muhammad al-Hajj Husayn Hadid, is a wealthy industrialist and political figure in Baghdad. Her mother, Wajiha al-Sabunji, is an artist from Mosul. Her brother Foulath is part of the household.

events.title: Studies Mathematics in Beirut
events.description: Hadid studies mathematics at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon. Her childhood visits to ancient Sumerian cities in southern Iraq have drawn her toward architecture and the built landscape.
events.background:
Baghdad’s political life had been part of Hadid’s family world before she entered university. Her father, Muhammad al-Hajj Husayn Hadid, had studied economics at the London School of Economics from 1928 to 1931. He returned to Iraq and joined the Ministry of Finance. In 1932, he helped found the al-Ahali group, which promoted public welfare and reform. The group resigned together in 1937 after General Bakr Sidqi sought dictatorial power following a coup. Muhammad Hadid later became vice president of the National Democratic Party. The party supported agrarian reform, workers’ rights, and state control of Iraq’s young oil industry.

After the 1958 Iraqi coup, Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim appointed Muhammad Hadid minister of finance. He used loans from the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe to support industrial projects and programs for Iraqis in poverty. He left the ministry in March 1960. A 1963 coup briefly brought the Ba’ath Party to power. Muhammad Hadid was tried, interned, and deprived of his assets. He turned his attention to business after a later coup.

The family’s intellectual interests also crossed art, politics, and international study. Hadid’s mother, Wajiha al-Sabunji, was an artist from Mosul. Her brother Foulath later recalled a home visited by leading figures in the National Democratic Party. During the 1960s, Hadid attended boarding schools in England and Switzerland. Her undergraduate work at the American University of Beirut preceded her move to London in 1972 for architectural training. At the Architectural Association, she treated painting as a design tool and used abstraction to revisit unrealized experiments in modern architecture. Her graduation project, Malevich’s Tektonik, was an acrylic-painted proposal for a 14-level hotel on London’s Hungerford Bridge, shaped by the work of the Suprematist artist Kazimir Malevich.

events.title: Moves to London
events.description: Hadid leaves Beirut for London to study at the Architectural Association School of Architecture, an architecture school in London. Rem Koolhaas, Elia Zenghelis, and Bernard Tschumi teach her there.
events.background:
The Architectural Association had become a center for radical ideas by the late 1960s. Elia Zenghelis said architecture was in crisis and that the search for new directions had shifted into schools. The AA brought architects including Coop Himmelblau and Adolfo Natalini of Superstudio to London. Zenghelis had been teaching there since 1963. He introduced a more radical avant-garde approach into the curriculum. Koolhaas had attended the same school from 1968 before pursuing further study at Cornell University and the Institute for Architecture and Urban Studies in New York.

The school offered a setting where architectural ideas could be developed through images as well as conventional building plans. Hadid sought an alternative to traditional architectural drawing. She used painting as a design tool. She drew on Suprematism and the Russian avant-garde, especially the work of Kazimir Malevich. Abstraction gave her a way to revisit experiments from modern architecture that she considered unfinished or untested. Her teachers saw an unusually expansive visual imagination. Koolhaas later called her “a planet in her own orbit.”

Zenghelis recalled calling her “the inventor of the 89 degrees” because nothing in her work settled at a right angle. He said her drawings broke buildings into tiny pieces. He also recalled that she focused on the overall spatial picture and gave little attention to practical details such as staircases. In his account, the constricted stair spaces in her drawings could send a visitor’s head into the ceiling. He believed construction details could be resolved later and said she was right. The AA’s atmosphere and its teachers’ circle led to work with Koolhaas and Zenghelis after her studies ended.

events.title: Graduates from the AA
events.description: At the Architectural Association School of Architecture in London, Hadid develops Malevich's Tektonik as her graduation thesis. The proposal places a 14-level hotel over Hungerford Bridge. She renders it as an acrylic painting shaped by [[Suprematism]], the abstract movement developed by Kazimir Malevich.

Suprematism.explanation: Kazimir Malevich developed Suprematism in Russia in the 1910s. It used geometric forms that did not depict recognizable objects.

events.title: Joins Office for Metropolitan Architecture
events.description: Hadid moves to Rotterdam to work with Rem Koolhaas and Elia Zenghelis at the [[Office for Metropolitan Architecture|Office for Metropolitan Architecture]], an architecture practice known as OMA. She meets Peter Rice, an architectural engineer, through Koolhaas. Rice supports her early career.

Office for Metropolitan Architecture.explanation: OMA is an international architecture practice founded in Rotterdam in 1975 by Rem Koolhaas, Elia Zenghelis, Zoe Zenghelis, and Madelon Vriesendorp.

events.title: Opens Her London Practice
events.description: In London, Hadid establishes Zaha Hadid Architects as her own practice. She develops proposals through large-scale paintings and drawings. Her work continues to use Suprematist ideas and angled, floating forms.

events.title: Appears in MoMA Exhibition
events.description: The Museum of Modern Art in New York includes Hadid among seven architects in the [[Deconstructivism in Architecture|Deconstructivism in Architecture exhibition]]. Philip Johnson and Mark Wigley curate the show. Their selection brings Hadid's projects to an international museum audience.

Deconstructivism in Architecture.explanation: Deconstructivism was a late-1980s architectural tendency associated with forms that appear fractured, tilted, or disrupted. The 1988 MoMA exhibition gave the tendency its best-known public label.

events.title: Completes Vitra Fire Station
events.description: Rolf Fehlbaum commissions Hadid to design a fire station for Vitra's campus in Weil am Rhein. The Vitra Fire Station opens in 1993 for the campus fire service. Raw concrete walls and sharp diagonal planes shape the building.

images.caption: Vitra Fire Station at Vitra Campus
images.creator: Marsupium

events.background:
Vitra’s factory campus at Weil am Rhein had become a place where a furniture company commissioned architects to make buildings for public attention as well as production. In 1989, Vitra had asked Frank Gehry, then little known, to design a design museum there. The fire-station project came as Hadid’s proposals were widely printed in architecture journals, although few had reached construction. Her standing rested on teaching, lectures, and paintings of projects whose angled forms broke conventional building geometry. The station gave those drawings a small, exacting practical test on an industrial site.

The completed structure treated the fire station as a sculptural arrangement. Concrete and glass were assembled in sharply angled elements that seem to collide at the center. Its walls and planes gave the building the compressed, directional quality of Hadid’s painted designs. The project had to house a working emergency service within Vitra’s campus, where the buildings also formed part of the company’s architectural collection. Its design plans had already appeared in architecture magazines before construction was finished.

Weil am Rhein soon opened its own municipal fire station. Vitra’s building consequently served its original emergency function for only a short time. It became an exhibition space, where it stands alongside work by Gehry and other architects on the campus. The building provided the first major built platform for Hadid’s architectural career. By the time she received the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2004, the jury noted that her completed body of work remained small and named the Vitra Fire Station among four finished buildings.

events.title: Opens Cincinnati Arts Center
events.description: The Contemporary Arts Center opens in Cincinnati with galleries and public spaces designed by Hadid. Her proposal wins the design competition, whose finalists include Rem Koolhaas. She becomes the first woman to design an art museum in the United States.

events.title: Wins Pritzker Prize
events.description: Hadid receives the [[Pritzker Architecture Prize]] at the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg. Thomas Pritzker announces the award. Hadid is its first woman recipient.

Pritzker Architecture Prize.explanation: The Pritzker Architecture Prize is an annual international award for an architect whose work has made significant contributions to the field.

events.background:
By 2004, architectural journals had made Hadid’s paintings and competition proposals familiar long before many of her designs reached construction. Her approach grew from Suprematism and the Russian avant-garde. At London’s Architectural Association, Rem Koolhaas, Elia Zenghelis, and Bernard Tschumi taught her. Her graduation project, Malevich’s Tektonik, proposed a 14-story hotel over Hungerford Bridge through an acrylic painting inspired by Kazimir Malevich. After graduating in 1977, she worked with Koolhaas and Zenghelis at the Office for Metropolitan Architecture in Rotterdam. She opened her London practice in 1980.

Her early public reputation rested heavily on lectures, drawings, and designs that clients did not build. The Peak leisure-club project in Hong Kong from 1983 became one of the best-known examples. A Cardiff opera-house scheme brought a painful setback in 1994. The competition jury selected her design, yet the Millennium Commission refused to fund it and gave the project to another architect. Hadid asked, “Do they want nothing but mediocrity?” The Museum of Modern Art raised her international profile in 1988 when Philip Johnson and Mark Wigley included her among seven architects in their Deconstructivism in Architecture exhibition.

The jury considered a built record that was still small. It included the Vitra Fire Station at Weil am Rhein, a sharply angled concrete and glass structure commissioned by Vitra’s Rolf Fehlbaum. The building served briefly as a fire station before the town opened its own facility. It then became an exhibition space alongside work by Frank Gehry and other designers. The Bergisel Ski Jump in Innsbruck combined a 48-meter jump with a 150-seat café and mountain views. Hadid called it an “organic hybrid” of bridge and tower. Her list also included the Hoenheim North parking garage and terminus in France and Cincinnati’s Contemporary Arts Center. Thomas Pritzker said her completed work was relatively small, while her energy and ideas gave greater promise for the future.

events.title: Opens MAXXI Museum
events.description: Rome opens the National Museum of Arts of the 21st Century, known as MAXXI, in a building designed by Hadid. Patrik Schumacher works with her at Zaha Hadid Architects. Intersecting galleries, stairs, and routes organize the museum interior.

events.title: Receives First Stirling Prize
events.description: The [[Royal Institute of British Architects|Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA)]] awards Hadid the [[Stirling Prize]] for MAXXI. The award recognizes the museum's architectural achievement in 2010.

Stirling Prize.explanation: The Stirling Prize is an annual British architecture award presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects for a building considered to have made the greatest contribution to British architecture that year.

Royal Institute of British Architects.explanation: RIBA is the United Kingdom's professional body for architects. It administers the Stirling Prize and awards the Royal Gold Medal.

events.title: Completes London Aquatics Centre
events.description: Hadid completes the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympic Games. The venue stands in London's Olympic Park. Its sweeping roof covers the competition pools and spectator seating.

events.title: Opens Broad Art Museum
events.description: Michigan State University opens its Eli and Edythe Broad Art Museum in East Lansing. Hadid designs its folded, angular building. Galleries, teaching spaces, and public routes sit within its pleated form.

images.caption: MSU Eli and Edythe Broad Art Museum
images.creator: Dj1997

events.background:
The commission came during a period when Hadid was designing large public buildings across several continents. Her completed projects already included museums in Cincinnati and Rome, an opera house in Guangzhou, and the London Aquatics Centre. The East Lansing building was her second project in the United States. It provided 4,274 square meters of space for contemporary art, modern art, and a historical collection.

The museum takes the form of a sharply leaning parallelogram. Its pleated exterior is clad in stainless steel. The angled surfaces catch views of the surrounding neighborhood from changing directions. Hadid wrote that the building’s appearance changes with the weather, the time of day, and the angle of sunlight. She described its effect as creating curiosity while withholding a full view of what is inside.

Elaine Glusac of The New York Times wrote that the architecture “radicalizes the streetscape.” The building later appeared in a scene in the 2016 film Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice.

events.title: Receives Royal Gold Medal
events.description: RIBA awards Hadid the [[Royal Gold Medal]] in London. She becomes the first woman to receive the medal as an individual recipient.

Royal Gold Medal.explanation: The Royal Gold Medal is RIBA's highest honor. It recognizes a person's work and influence in architecture.

events.title: Death in Miami
events.description: Hadid is receiving treatment for [[bronchitis]] at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami. A heart attack occurs during her treatment.
